query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, small amounts of element-specific segregation that occur during service (or controlled thermal exposure) can locally lower grain-boundary cohesion by triggering nanoscale intermetallic formation, which in turn produces brittle failure modes that are distinct from the ductile mechanisms observed in as-solidified alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy prepared via arc melting and homogenization, exhibiting a uniform microstructure and excellent ductility with no detectable secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging treatment designed to accelerate grain-boundary segregation without inducing gross grain coarsening. The treatment is executed by holding samples at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 800°C) for a period sufficient to induce localized segregation but below the temperature that triggers rapid grain growth.
generation.conditions: After aging, samples are tested at room temperature under standard fracture toughness tests (e.g., compact tension specimens under monotonic loading at a moderate strain rate) to simulate service conditions. For comparison, baseline samples are maintained without the aging treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale formation of intermetallic precipitates located at grain boundaries resulting from local compositional fluctuations due to segregation.
generation.mechanism: Diffusion-driven segregation of specific alloying elements (possibly those with a high propensity to form intermetallic phases) accumulates at grain boundaries during the thermal treatment. This localized enrichment lowers the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries by initiating nanoscale precipitation that acts as crack initiation sites, thus promoting an intergranular (brittle) fracture mode, which contrasts with the transgranular, ductile fracture seen in the unaged state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial uniform, ductile single-phase alloy, the thermally aged alloy will show a decrease in toughness, evidenced by lower fracture toughness values and a shift to more intergranular fracture behavior during mechanical testing.
generation.baseline: As-solidified, homogenized high-entropy alloy demonstrating excellent ductility and toughness with predominantly transgranular crack propagation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is relevant under service conditions that include moderate thermal exposures (around 800°C for periods that permit grain-boundary segregation) followed by mechanical loading at or near room temperature. It assumes that the alloy remains compositionally complex and single-phase in the bulk.
generation.uncertainty: The rate and extent of segregation, as well as the critical concentration required to trigger embrittling intermetallic formation, may vary with minor alloying additions and processing history. It is also unclear how competing mechanisms such as strain-induced grain-boundary stabilization might interact.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two nearly identical sets of high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the controlled thermal aging treatment (e.g., 800°C for a specified period) expected to induce grain-boundary segregation, while keeping the other set as a baseline control. Following treatment, perform identical fracture toughness tests (e.g., compact tension specimens tested at room temperature under monotonic loading) and analyze the fracture surfaces via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to classify the failure mode (intergranular vs. transgranular).
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (degree of intergranular cracking)
Grain-boundary chemistry via localized compositional analysis (e.g., EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness, nor a visible enhancement of intergranular fracture features compared to the baseline, or if no evidence of grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale intermetallics is detected, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary segregation leads to embrittlement in high-entropy alloys would be falsified.
